winners.premise: A groom keeps the wedding reception his ex-fiancée paid for, marries another woman, and asks his ex to approve the final bill.
winners.conflict: An ex-fiancée must refuse to fund a replacement wedding while the groom uses both the existing booking and his new wife's feelings to pressure her.
winners.twist: The new bride was told the canceled wedding had been settled and that the groom's family paid for this reception.
winners.hook: A groom used his ex-fiancée's money to marry someone else. Then he asked his ex to sign the final bill.
winners.narration: Claire walked into the reception after the venue called to confirm her final payment. Daniel was wearing the suit they'd chosen together. The woman beside him was wearing a wedding dress. He hurried over and asked Claire to keep her voice down. Two weeks earlier, he'd ended their engagement and told her he'd canceled everything. Claire asked about the six thousand she'd paid for food and the room. Daniel said the arrangements couldn't go to waste just because they'd broken up. The coordinator brought over the bill, still under Claire's name. Daniel said signing it would be easier than making everyone wait while they changed the booking details. Claire said she wasn't authorizing another charge. His new wife, Elise, came over and asked who she was. Daniel called her the person who'd helped arrange the reception. Claire said she'd been the bride who paid for it. Elise looked at Daniel. He'd told her the old wedding was settled and his parents were paying for this one. Daniel asked Claire why she needed to hurt someone who'd done nothing wrong. Claire said he could have protected Elise by telling her the truth before inviting her into a wedding someone else funded. She put the unsigned bill on the table. The coordinator asked Daniel how he would pay the balance. He reached for Claire's pen. She took it with her. He could keep the flowers. He wasn't keeping her signature.
winners.title: The Bride Changed. Her Name Stayed on the Bill.
winners.description: A canceled engagement leaves one woman paying for a reception with a different bride.
winners.like_cta: LIKE IF HIS WEDDING WAS HIS BILL

winners.premise: A father tells his son that Grandma died after becoming estranged from her, then asks his living mother to pretend to be a stranger when they meet.
winners.conflict: A grandmother must correct a cruel lie without making her grandson carry the adults' dispute or demanding affection from him.
winners.twist: The father turned anger over his mother's divorce into a false death story, leaving the child to grieve someone who was still alive.
winners.hook: A father lied to his son that Grandma had died. Now he wanted his living mother to pretend to be a stranger.
winners.narration: Eva heard Ben say her name in the supermarket. Her son, Mark, stepped between them and whispered that she should say she was an old neighbor. Ben had been through enough confusion. The boy asked why she looked like the photograph beside his bed. Mark said they needed to go. Eva stayed where she was and told Ben she was his grandmother. He asked whether people could come back from heaven. Mark said the boy had misunderstood something he'd said when he was upset. Ben said Dad had told him Grandma was in heaven with their dog. Eva asked Mark to explain that part himself. He looked at his son and admitted she hadn't died. Ben asked whether she'd gone away because of him. Eva said the argument had been between adults. She'd divorced his grandfather, and his dad had been angry about it. Nothing Ben had done caused that. Mark told her not to bring the family dispute into a supermarket. She said the dispute hadn't made Ben think someone he loved was dead. The story he'd told had done that. Ben asked whether he could call her. Eva said she'd answer, then waited for Mark to tell him how. He put her number into his phone and handed it to Ben. Eva's phone rang while they stood beside each other. Ben said hello, Grandma. The call lasted ten seconds. The lie had lasted two years.
winners.title: Grandma Wasn't in Heaven
winners.description: An unexpected meeting forces a father to explain the death story he told his child.
winners.payoff: The call lasted ten seconds. The lie had lasted two years.
winners.like_cta: LIKE IF BEN DESERVED THE TRUTH

winners.premise: A boss demands the winning lottery ticket he gave his cleaner, but she has already given it to a delivery driver as a tip.
winners.conflict: A cleaner must decide whether a life-changing prize justifies breaking her promise when her boss threatens her job over the ticket.
winners.twist: The cleaner wants the ticket back too, but refuses to steal it from the person she freely gave it to.
winners.hook: A boss demanded the winning lottery ticket he'd given his cleaner. She'd already tipped the delivery driver with it.
winners.narration: Rina had left her purse upstairs when the driver helped carry a parcel inside. She gave him the staff-party ticket from her pocket instead. He thanked her and tucked it into his jacket. That afternoon, her boss, Colin, checked the numbers on the tickets he'd bought. Rina's had won half a million dollars. He told her to bring the driver back. Rina called him, but said he should check his ticket. When he returned, Colin said company gifts were company property until he approved what happened to them. The driver asked Rina whether she'd meant to give it away. She said yes. Colin pointed to the jacket the driver had left on a chair while helping unload another parcel. He told Rina to take the ticket before the man came inside. She said no. Colin told her she'd lose her job over money that should have been theirs. Rina said she'd been thinking about getting it back since she heard the amount. That didn't make it something she could take. Colin told her to clear her locker. The driver returned and heard why she was leaving. He asked whether she regretted giving him the ticket. Rina said she regretted not checking it. She hadn't changed what she'd meant when she handed it over. He took a five-dollar note from his wallet and offered it to thank her for calling. The ticket stayed in his pocket. The tip stayed in hers.
winners.title: The Tip in the Delivery Driver's Pocket
winners.description: A lottery win turns a small gift into a test of what one worker is willing to take back.
winners.payoff: The ticket stayed in his pocket. The tip stayed in hers.
winners.like_cta: LIKE IF A GIFT STAYS A GIFT

winners.premise: A locksmith sells a man's new house key to his ex-girlfriend after being hired to keep her out.
winners.conflict: A homeowner must reclaim control over access to his home when the service provider treats a higher payment as permission to override his instructions.
winners.twist: The ex-girlfriend refuses to return the key because she paid for it, leaving the homeowner to choose a different provider and someone he actually trusts with a spare.
winners.hook: A man caught his locksmith selling his new house key to his ex-girlfriend. He'd hired him to keep her out.
winners.narration: Tom came back with his wallet and saw Gary handing Lena a key. She'd moved out and returned her old one the previous week. Tom asked what Gary was doing. The locksmith said she'd paid for an extra copy so she could collect her things. Tom had already arranged a Saturday pickup while he was home. Lena said she'd rather come when it suited her. Gary said this was a personal disagreement and he was only providing a service. Tom asked which customer had authorized that service. Gary said Lena had paid two hundred dollars, more than Tom's original callout. Lena put the key in her pocket. She wasn't giving it back unless someone refunded her. Gary asked Tom whether he'd cover that so they could all move on. Tom told him to stop working. Gary offered to change the lock again for free if Tom didn't leave a bad review. Tom said he needed a locksmith whose work he could trust when he left the room. He called another firm. His neighbor, Mo, came over and stayed with him while the new lock was fitted. Lena left with the key she'd bought. It no longer opened his door. Afterward, Tom asked Mo whether she'd keep a spare for emergencies. She said she'd knock before using it unless he needed help. He handed her the copy. This spare went to someone he'd actually asked.
winners.title: Who Bought His New House Key?
winners.description: A locksmith takes a second payment that defeats the reason he was hired.
winners.payoff: This spare went to someone he'd actually asked.
